Too many meetings and not enough hours. Eleven meetings in three days.
Eleven? How much time does that leave you for the actual work?
Almost none. I do the real tasks after seven, when everybody runs out of questions.
That is not a lot of life for one person. Do you get any help?
I have a few good people on my team, and they handle a lot. But there is only one of me. And you? How is the new job?
Quieter. Less money, more space in my head, and a lot more energy at seven. I have enough for what I need and I go home at six.
That sounds like a lot more than enough. Give me some advice: how did you decide?
I have a few good people on my team, and they handle a lot.
I have enough for what I need, and I go home at six.
And you? How much free time do you have this week?

I counted, because I did not believe it myself. In one week I was in twenty-three meetings. Twenty-three. Some of them were nine minutes long, which is worse than an hour, because nine minutes takes the whole hour anyway. I did not do any real work between Monday and Thursday. I answered a lot of questions, I made a few decisions, and I read almost nothing. So on the Friday I did something I should have done years earlier. I cancelled everything that did not have a decision in it, and I put two hours in the calendar every morning with no name on them. People asked what those two hours were. I said they were a meeting. Nobody has ever asked me who else is in it.

I took a job that pays less, and everybody asked me the same question with the same face. How much less? About twenty per cent. And what nobody ever asked, which is the part that actually matters, is how much more of everything else. I have more time, more energy at seven in the evening, and a lot more patience with my daughter, who did not do anything wrong and used to get whatever was left of me. I am not going to pretend money does not matter. It matters a great deal, and there is a number below which none of this works at all. But I was well above that number, and I was still saying yes to everything, because more was the only direction I knew. Enough is a real amount. It is just very hard to see from where I was standing.

Here is something nobody tells you about energy. It does not run out at the end of the day. It runs out at the point where you stop choosing what to spend it on. I can work for nine hours and go home fine. I cannot do four hours of things somebody else decided for me. And the two feel identical while you are doing them, which is exactly why people blame the number of hours. So count something else for a week. Not how many hours you worked. How many of them you chose. If the answer is almost none, then the problem is not the amount of work. And if the answer is most of them and you are still exhausted, then it really is the amount, and that is a completely different conversation with a completely different person.
